$comment: Source shapes the linker has to carry, and what each one must evaluate to.
Ruvyxa's linker is its own — no esbuild, no Rollup — and it rewrites ESM one
statement at a time rather than parsing to an AST and printing it back. That
is a deliberate trade, and its failure mode is narrow and quiet: a construct
the rewriter does not recognise is copied through, and the bundle either
fails to parse or, worse, parses and means something else.
Every entry below is a shape that reached this file because it broke
something, or because it is one step away from a shape that did. Four were
found by running this table for the first time:
- `export { source as from }` was read as a re-export and dropped silently
- top-level await produced a bundle that would not parse
- a decorator written inline survived into the output
- a leading `#!` line did the same
`expect` is what the linked bundle must *evaluate to*, not what it must look
like. Half of the defects this table exists for produced output that compiled
cleanly and computed the wrong answer, and only running it catches those.
Replayed by tests/packages/ruvyxa/module-syntax.test.mjs, which compiles and
runs each case, and by the `mod syntax_conformance_tests` in
crates/ruvyxa_bundler/src/linker.rs, which links each dependency and checks
that nothing was left behind. Adding a case is one entry here.

cases.name: regex with a slash inside a character class
cases.dependency: export const hit = "a/b".replace(/[/]/g, "-")
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: The `/` inside the class does not end the literal. Reading it as the end leaves `]/g` as code.

cases.name: regex containing a backtick
cases.dependency: export const hit = "a`b".replace(/[`]/g, "-")
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: A backtick inside a regex must not open a template literal.

cases.name: regex containing a quote
cases.dependency: export const pattern = /it's/
cases.entry:
import { pattern } from './dep.js'
export const value = String(pattern.test("it's"))
cases.why: The quote is regex content. Reading it as a string opener ran to the next quote in the file.

cases.name: regex with an escaped slash
cases.dependency: export const hit = "a/b".replace(/\//, "-")
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: An escaped delimiter does not end the literal.

cases.name: division after a closing paren is not a regex
cases.dependency: export const hit = (10) / 2 + 1
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = String(hit)
cases.why: A `/` after a value is division. Treating it as a regex swallows the rest of the line.

cases.name: division after an identifier ending in a keyword
cases.dependency:
const inreturn = 10
export const hit = inreturn / 2
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = String(hit)
cases.why: `return` is a keyword; `inreturn` is not. A prefix match would call this a regex position.

cases.name: regex directly after return
cases.dependency: export function test(v) { return /^a/.test(v) }
cases.entry:
import { test } from './dep.js'
export const value = String(test('abc'))
cases.why: A `/` after a keyword is a regex, which is the other half of the previous case.

cases.name: nested template literals with interpolation
cases.dependency:
const inner = "x"
export const hit = `a${`b${inner}c`}d`
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: The inner template must not end the outer one.

cases.name: escaped backtick inside a template literal
cases.dependency: export const hit = `a\`b`
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = String(hit.length)
cases.why: An escaped delimiter does not end the literal.

cases.name: template literal spanning lines with an export inside
cases.dependency:
export const hit = `line one
export const decoy = 2
line three`
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = String(hit.split('\n').length)
cases.why: A statement-shaped line inside template text is text. A line-based rewriter has to be told.

cases.name: top-level await in a dependency
cases.dependency: export const hit = await Promise.resolve("awaited")
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: Every module is wrapped in a function, and `await` is illegal in a synchronous one.

cases.name: top-level await in the entry
cases.dependency: export const hit = "dynamic"
cases.entry:
const m = await import('./dep.js')
export const value = m.hit
cases.why: Awaiting a dynamic import at the top of a route is ordinary and hit the same wrapper.

cases.name: for await at the top level
cases.dependency: export async function* steps() { yield 5 }
cases.entry:
import { steps } from './dep.js'
let total = 0
for await (const n of steps()) total += n
export const value = String(total)
cases.why: The same wrapper problem, reached through a different keyword.

cases.name: generator export
cases.dependency: export function* steps() { yield 1; yield 2 }
cases.entry:
import { steps } from './dep.js'
export const value = [...steps()].join(',')
cases.why: The `*` binds to the keyword, so a prefix list written as `export function ` misses it.

cases.name: export aliased to `from`
cases.dependency:
const source = 1
export { source as from }
cases.entry:
import { from } from './dep.js'
export const value = String(from)
cases.why: `from` is a keyword only where a specifier follows it, and an ordinary binding name otherwise.

cases.name: multi-line export list
cases.entry:
import { a, b } from './dep.js'
export const value = String(a + b)
cases.why: A clause wrapped across lines is one statement; rewriting only its first line leaves tokens behind.

cases.name: multi-line import list
cases.dependency:
export const a = 1
export const b = 2
cases.why: The import half of the same problem.

cases.name: re-export from another module
cases.dependency: export const hit = "through"
cases.entry: export { hit as value } from './dep.js'
cases.why: The form the `from` guard must still recognise.

cases.name: namespace import
cases.dependency: export const hit = "ns"
cases.entry:
import * as all from './dep.js'
export const value = all.hit
cases.why: A namespace binding is the module object, not its default.

cases.name: destructured export with a default value
cases.dependency:
const source = { a: 1 }
export const { a, b = 9 } = source
cases.entry:
import { a, b } from './dep.js'
export const value = String(a + b)
cases.why: A destructuring declaration binds several names and matches no single-name pattern.

cases.name: array destructured export
cases.dependency: export const [first, second] = [1, 2]
cases.entry:
import { first, second } from './dep.js'
export const value = String(first + second)
cases.why: The array form of the same declaration.

cases.name: export default arrow spanning lines
cases.entry:
import twice from './dep.js'
export const value = String(twice(4))
cases.why: A default export whose expression continues past its first line.

cases.name: export default class with a name
cases.dependency: export default class Named { run() { return "classy" } }
cases.entry:
import Named from './dep.js'
export const value = new Named().run()
cases.why: The declaration form of a default export, which keeps its binding.

cases.name: export default an object literal spanning lines
cases.entry:
import shape from './dep.js'
export const value = String(shape.a + shape.b)
cases.why: The expression form, wrapped.

cases.name: two statements sharing one line
cases.dependency: export const a = 1; export const b = 2
cases.entry:
import { a, b } from './dep.js'
export const value = String(a + b)
cases.why: A line-based rewriter sees one line and has to find both statements in it.

cases.name: object property named import
cases.dependency: export const hit = { import: "kept", export: "also" }.import
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: A reserved word is a valid property name and is not a statement.

cases.name: string containing an export statement
cases.dependency: export const hit = "export const fake = 1"
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit.slice(0, 6)
cases.why: Statement-shaped text inside a string is text.

cases.name: labelled statement
cases.dependency: export function run() { outer: for (const x of [1]) { break outer } return "looped" }
cases.entry:
import { run } from './dep.js'
export const value = run()
cases.why: `name:` is a label, not an object key or a type annotation.

cases.name: class with a private field
cases.dependency: export class Box { #v = 7; read() { return this.#v } }
cases.entry:
import { Box } from './dep.js'
export const value = String(new Box().read())
cases.why: `#` starts a private name here and a shebang at the top of a file; both reach the same scanner.

cases.name: class static block
cases.dependency: export class Reg { static seen = 0; static { Reg.seen = 3 } }
cases.entry:
import { Reg } from './dep.js'
export const value = String(Reg.seen)
cases.why: A brace block that is neither a function body nor an object literal.

cases.name: shebang at the top of a module
cases.dependency:
#!/usr/bin/env node
export const hit = "shebang"
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: Legal at the top of a module, illegal inside the wrapper every module is emitted into.

cases.name: BOM at the start of a module
cases.dependency: export const hit = "bom"
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: A byte-order mark before the first statement must not hide it.

cases.name: CRLF line endings
cases.dependency:
export const a = 1
export const b = 2
cases.entry:
import { a, b } from './dep.js'
export const value = String(a + b)
cases.why: A carriage return is trailing whitespace, not part of the statement.

cases.name: unicode identifier export
cases.dependency: export const café = "unicode"
cases.entry:
import { café } from './dep.js'
export const value = café
cases.why: An ASCII-only identifier pattern truncated the name and published a binding nothing declared.

cases.name: comment containing an apostrophe
cases.dependency:
// don't stop here
export const hit = 'ok'
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: An unmatched quote in prose is not a delimiter.

cases.name: block comment containing a template and a regex
cases.dependency:
/* `${x}` and /y/g */
export const hit = "ok"
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: Neither construct starts inside a comment.

cases.name: comment ending in a backslash
cases.dependency:
// trailing backslash \
export const hit = "after-comment"
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: A line comment ends at the newline; a backslash does not continue it.

cases.name: escaped quote inside a string
cases.dependency:
export const first = "he said \"hi\""
export const second = "after"
cases.entry:
import { second } from './dep.js'
export const value = second
cases.why: An escaped quote does not close the string.

cases.name: line continuation inside a string
cases.dependency:
export const hit = "one\
two"
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: A backslash before a newline continues the string onto the next line.

cases.name: import.meta is available
cases.dependency: export const hit = typeof import.meta.url
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: `import.meta` is not an import statement, and a bundled module still needs one.

cases.name: optional chaining call on an imported function
cases.dependency: export const maybe = () => "called"
cases.entry:
import { maybe } from './dep.js'
export const value = maybe?.() ?? 'missing'
cases.why: A rewritten binding has to stay callable through the optional form.

cases.name: dynamic import of a sibling
cases.dependency: export const hit = "dynamic"
cases.entry:
const m = await import('./dep.js')
export const value = m.hit
cases.why: A dynamic specifier resolves to a bundled module rather than a network request.

cases.name: type-only import is erased
cases.dependency:
export type Shape = { a: number }
export const hit = "kept"
cases.entry:
import type { Shape } from './dep.ts'
import { hit } from './dep.ts'
const s: Shape = { a: 1 }
export const value = hit + s.a
cases.why: A type-only import names no runtime binding and must not become one.

cases.name: inline type modifier in a named import
cases.dependency:
export type Shape = { a: number }
export const hit = "kept"
cases.why: One clause carrying both a type and a value.

cases.name: export type is erased
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.ts'
export const value = hit
cases.why: `export type` publishes nothing at runtime and must not emit an assignment.

cases.name: satisfies operator
cases.dependency: export const hit = { a: 1 } satisfies Record<string, number>
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.ts'
export const value = String(hit.a)
cases.why: A type-level operator in the middle of a value declaration.

cases.name: const type parameter on a generic arrow
cases.dependency: export const identity = <const T,>(value: T): T => value
cases.entry:
import { identity } from './dep.ts'
export const value = identity('generic')
cases.why: Angle brackets that are not JSX and not a comparison.

cases.name: generic type argument at a call site
cases.dependency: export function pick<T>(list: T[]): T { return list[0] }
cases.entry:
import { pick } from './dep.ts'
export const value = pick<string>(['first', 'second'])
cases.why: The same ambiguity read from the calling side.

cases.name: enum export
cases.dependency: export enum Level { Low = 1, High = 2 }
cases.entry:
import { Level } from './dep.ts'
export const value = String(Level.High)
cases.why: An enum is a runtime value with a declaration form the rewriter has to recognise.

cases.name: const enum export
cases.dependency: export const enum Flag { On = 3 }
cases.entry:
import { Flag } from './dep.ts'
export const value = String(Flag.On)
cases.why: `export const enum` reads as `export const` up to the keyword after it.

cases.name: namespace export
cases.dependency: export namespace Tools { export const name = "ns" }
cases.entry:
import { Tools } from './dep.ts'
export const value = Tools.name
cases.why: A namespace body holds exports of its own that are not module exports.

cases.name: abstract class and its implementation
cases.dependency:
export abstract class Base { abstract go(): string }
export class Impl extends Base { go() { return "went" } }
cases.entry:
import { Impl } from './dep.ts'
export const value = new Impl().go()
cases.why: `export abstract class` is a declaration prefix of its own.

cases.name: constructor parameter property
cases.dependency: export class Holder { constructor(public readonly name: string) {} }
cases.entry:
import { Holder } from './dep.ts'
export const value = new Holder('held').name
cases.why: A modifier in a parameter list that becomes a field assignment.

cases.name: decorator on a class method
cases.dependency:
function log(_t: unknown, _k: string, d: PropertyDescriptor) { return d }
export class Svc { @log run() { return "ran" } }
cases.entry:
import { Svc } from './dep.ts'
export const value = new Svc().run()
cases.why: Written inline, which is what a formatter produces for a short member and what minified code always has.

cases.name: non-null assertion
cases.dependency: export const maybe: string | null = "present"
cases.entry:
import { maybe } from './dep.ts'
export const value = maybe!.toUpperCase()
cases.why: A `!` that is a type assertion rather than negation.

cases.name: as const assertion
cases.dependency: export const list = ["a", "b"] as const
cases.entry:
import { list } from './dep.ts'
export const value = list.join('')
cases.why: A type assertion after a value, on the same line as the declaration.

cases.name: template literal type
cases.dependency:
type Path = `/${string}`
export const hit: Path = "/root"
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.ts'
export const value = hit
cases.why: A template literal in type position, which is erased rather than evaluated.

cases.name: a non-ASCII identifier declared at top level
cases.dependency:
const café = 'brewed'
export const hit = café
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: The linker collects top-level bound names by walking bytes and slicing at each position. A position inside a multi-byte character is not a slice boundary, so this aborted the build with a Rust panic rather than any diagnostic.

cases.name: a non-ASCII identifier exported under an ASCII alias
cases.dependency:
const ค่า = 'thai'
export { ค่า as hit }
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: The export clause has to carry a local name the ASCII identifier scan cannot spell. Dropping it makes the binding undefined at the import site with nothing reported.

cases.name: division whose left operand ends in a non-ASCII character
cases.dependency: const π = 2;const q = 10 / π;const half = q / π;const note = 'a/b';export const hit = String(half) + note
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: A `/` after a Unicode identifier is a division. Both scanners read it as a regular-expression opener and blanked everything to the next `/` — on one line, which is what a minified dependency is, that swallows real code.

cases.name: a non-ASCII character inside a string next to a division
cases.dependency: const label = 'café';const half = 10 / 2;export const hit = label + half
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: The same bytes as the case above, in text rather than in code. The classification must come from the token before the slash, not from anywhere on the line.

cases.name: a string literal continued onto the next line
cases.dependency:
const help = "run \
import x from 'ghost'"
export const hit = help
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.js'
export const value = hit
cases.why: A backslash at the end of a line continues the literal, so this is one string and its text is not code. Walking it as code turned the words inside into a dependency edge on a module named `ghost`.

cases.name: a generic arrow function in a TypeScript module
cases.dependency:
export const identity = <T>(value: T): T => value
export const hit = identity('generic')
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.ts'
export const value = hit
cases.why: `<T>` is a type parameter in a `.ts` file and an element in a `.tsx` one. The client graph switched JSX on from its own scan, so this ordinary TypeScript stopped parsing there while the server graph compiled it.

cases.name: an angle-bracket type assertion in a TypeScript module
cases.dependency:
const raw: unknown = 'asserted'
export const hit = <string>raw
cases.entry:
import { hit } from './dep.ts'
export const value = hit
cases.why: The other form the `.tsx` reading destroys. TypeScript settles both by extension and never by contents.
